statement: In healthy volunteers, whether the liver enzyme CYP2D6 works changed MDMA's blood level only a little, and medicines that block the enzyme raised it by a similar small amount; the authors link this to MDMA itself switching the enzyme off, which a probe-drug study found lasting for days. In a pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 139 people, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 (poor metabolizers, all given the higher dose) had a peak MDMA level 15% higher than the 111 with normal function (mean ratio 1.15), a peak of the active metabolite MDA 50% higher and a peak of the inactive metabolite HMMA 50 to 70% lower; the MDMA difference was confined to the first 3 hours, and their effects came sooner but were not larger at the maximum (Schmid et al., 2016). In 15 men with normal CYP2D6 given a test drug (dextromethorphan) before and after one dose of MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, the test drug's blood exposure rose roughly 9-fold (editors' calculation from the printed means; the authors say approximately 10-fold), the urinary ratio of the test drug to its product rose from 0.006 to 0.43, 67% (10 of the 15 men, by the editors' count) crossed the cut-off for poor metabolizers, and the ratio had not fully recovered after 10 days (recovery half-life 47 hours on one fit, 103 hours on another); the first test dose came 4 hours after MDMA and there was no placebo session, so, in the editors' reading, early competition for the enzyme cannot be told from its inactivation (O'Mathuna et al., 2008). In 12 men, paroxetine, which blocks CYP2D6 as well as the serotonin transporter, raised the MDMA peak by 16% and the exposure by 22% and lowered HMMA by 39 to 49% (Farre et al., 2007). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion raised the MDMA peak by 14 to 18%, and ritonavir, a strong enzyme blocker, was named as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (reports not read here); a 2012 narrative review by authors of the probe-drug and paroxetine studies says that the genotype and CYP2D6-blocking medicines may matter less for acute toxicity than once thought (de la Torre et al., 2012). Bodies that differ are one reason people can feel little from an amount and take more, alongside a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product and a medicine that blunts the effect; here the difference between bodies was small and early, and the effects came sooner, not stronger. What happens when people then take more was not tested, but the authors of the probe-drug study infer that a second dose taken while the enzyme is still switched off would reach higher concentrations (O'Mathuna et al., 2008). Only 7 people lacked CYP2D6 function, the probe-drug study included men only, and none of these studies gave a second dose of MDMA.
plain: The liver enzyme CYP2D6 helps clear MDMA, and bodies differ in how well it works. In a pooled lab analysis, the 7 people with no working CYP2D6 had only about 15 percent more MDMA in the blood at the peak, in the first 3 hours, and felt effects sooner, not stronger. The authors link this to MDMA switching the enzyme off itself: in 15 men a single MDMA dose pushed 10 of them into the range of people with no working enzyme, and it had not fully recovered after 10 days. Medicines that block the enzyme, such as paroxetine, raised MDMA by about 15 to 20 percent at the peak. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; bodies that differ are one reason, next to a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, or a medicine that mutes the effect. These small studies in healthy volunteers did not test that: none gave a second dose of MDMA. The authors of one study think that a second dose taken while the enzyme is still switched off would reach higher blood levels.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in controlled laboratory studies: 139 people (70 men, 69 women; 7 poor, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers) pooled from 8 studies; 15 men who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening; and 12 men, all extensive metabolizers
exposure: No working CYP2D6 (poor-metabolizer genotype); MDMA itself (a single dose, followed by a CYP2D6 probe drug); or a CYP2D6-blocking medicine (paroxetine for 3 days) (study conditions: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg or 100 mg; doses in the pooled analysis are in a supplement that was not read)
comparator: People with normal CYP2D6 function; the same men before MDMA (a control session with the probe drug alone, always first, no placebo MDMA); the same men after placebo instead of paroxetine
outcome: Peak and exposure of MDMA and its metabolites MDA and HMMA; blood levels of a CYP2D6 probe drug and the urinary probe-drug to metabolite ratio as measures of CYP2D6 activity, and time to recovery of that ratio; early effects
magnitude: Pooled genotype comparison (Schmid et al., 2016): peak MDMA 15% higher in 7 poor metabolizers (mean ratio 1.15 against 111 extensive; peak F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02; area to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01), peak MDA +50% (P<0.01), peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (P=0.03), early systolic pressure rise and liking higher at 0.6 hours, maximal effects not different. Probe drug (O'Mathuna et al., 2008, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL and area 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9; urinary ratio 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), 67% above the 0.3 cut-off; recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) one-phase, 103.0 hours (SD 70.3) two-phase; not fully recovered at 10 days. Paroxetine (Farre et al., 2007, n=12): MDMA peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and exposure to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L (both P<0.01); HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and exposure 1189.47 against 1923.32 (both P<0.01). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022): duloxetine peak +14.6%, reboxetine +17.8%, bupropion +14.3% with exposure to 24 hours +33.1%.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, limitations paragraph
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies in 139 healthy people (70 men, 69 women): 7 CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive metabolizers (111 extensive in one Discussion comparison). Doses and study details are in a supplement that was not read; all seven poor metabolizers were in the high-dose group, and the authors state that an analysis of the high-dose group alone gave similar results (no figures are given in the text).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
evidence.extracted: Genotype altered MDMA levels only in the first 3 hours (absorption and distribution), not after: genotype main effect on peak MDMA F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02, with higher peaks in poor than extensive metabolizers (P=0.049); area under the curve to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01 (poor higher than extensive, P<0.01). Peak MDMA was 15% higher in poor metabolizers (abstract) and the mean ratio was 1.15 (7 poor against 111 extensive).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend
evidence.extracted: The active metabolite MDA was higher and the inactive metabolite HMMA lower in poor metabolizers: peak MDA +50% (F(2,136)=8.82, P<0.01; area F=9.09, P<0.001); peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (F(2,73)=3.50, P=0.03; area F=5.22, P<0.01), HMMA exposure to 6 hours about a quarter (24%) of extensive metabolizers'; MDMA to HMMA ratios higher in poor metabolizers (F(2,73)=10.98 and 10.08, P<0.001). The HMMA tests rest on fewer people than the MDMA and MDA tests: N=76 in the HMMA correlation and F tests with 73 error degrees of freedom, against 136 for MDMA and MDA.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 2 legend; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
evidence.extracted: Poor metabolizers had faster early effects but not larger ones: systolic pressure rise greater than in intermediate (P=0.02) and extensive (P=0.01) metabolizers at 0.6 h (F(2,135)=3.50, P=0.03), 'any drug effect' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.05) and 'drug liking' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.001) and 1 h (P<0.01); maximal effects did not differ and there was no genotype effect on heart rate or temperature. The authors read the small, short-lived difference as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, turning all people into functional poor metabolizers within about 1 hour; they cite a model estimating a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function, and say medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 raised peak MDMA by 15 to 20% and exposure by 10 to 30%. They also note that poor metabolizers were not over-represented among ecstasy deaths (their reference 11), that severe or fatal toxicity with high MDMA exposure occurred with ritonavir, which blocks CYP2D6, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 (more than one enzyme system), and suggest that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics; no toxicity outcome was measured in the analysis.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 526); Drugs, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 526-527)
evidence.extracted: Fifteen healthy men (mean age 26, range 19 to 33; on average 26 previous MDMA experiences) who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening, recruited by word of mouth and paid. Open, fixed-order design: session 1 (control, dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg), then at least 3 days later session 2 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 75 to 100 mg, with caffeine and dextromethorphan 30 mg at 4 hours and later); the dextromethorphan schedule was 4, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 168 hours in the first 3 men and 4, 24, 72, 96, 168 and 240 hours in the other 12, because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; results pooled. No placebo MDMA session.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
evidence.extracted: Plasma probe drug after MDMA against the control session (Table 1, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL (SDs 3.6 and 18.5) and area over 8 hours 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9 and area 1877.1 to 179.1; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 to 16.6 and area 764.2 to 97.5 (all P<0.05); 3-methoxymorphinan not significantly changed. The authors say the dextromethorphan peak and area increased approximately 10-fold. MDMA peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0). Editors' calculation from the printed means: 8.5-fold for the peak and 9.5-fold for the area.

evidence.locator: Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2
evidence.extracted: The urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio rose from 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), which the authors call almost 100-fold; 67% of the men had a value above 0.3, the cut-off for assigning the poor-metabolizer phenotype, after MDMA; no correlation of the ratio with urine pH (r=0.049) or creatinine (r=0.214). Recovery fitted one exponential curve: rate constant 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour, recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791. Editors' calculation: the ratio of the printed means is 71-fold, and 67% of 15 men is 10 men.

The ratio had not recovered fully to its basal level at 10 days; the half-life corrected for MDMA's own residence time is 37.4 hours (SD 11.6), and the authors think it underestimates recovery because activity had not recovered even at 10 days; a two-phase fit gives 103.0 hours (SD 70.3), corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4), though variability and few time points question the biphasic model. Editors' reading: the first probe dose after MDMA was given 4 hours after it, when MDMA was near its peak, so competition for the enzyme cannot be separated from its inactivation in the early hours.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Table 2 (p. 961)
evidence.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine, an inhibitor of CYP2D6 as well as of the serotonin transporter, against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01). The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

evidence.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results › MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine; Discussion › Pharmacokinetic interactions-MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%; reboxetine: peak +17.8%; bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower; carvedilol, clonidine, doxazosin and methylphenidate changed the peak by 5% or less (memantine's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower). The Discussion names the strong enzyme blocker ritonavir as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (Papaseit et al., 2012, not read).

evidence.locator: Introduction > MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacogenetics and MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary of Schmid et al. (2016): people with only non-functional alleles (*3, *4, *5) had a peak MDMA level 19% higher and early exposure (to 6 hours) 25% higher than people with only *1 and *2 alleles, with faster onset and higher blood pressure; the review's 19% and 25% are for a narrower genotype comparison than the paper's headline 15% and are not reconciled with it (the paper's supplement was not read). Pooled trial data are said to show that effects follow plasma concentration and that higher CYP2D6 activity scores predict lower MDMA levels (Studerus et al., 2021, not read).

evidence.locator: MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon, paragraph 1; Abstract; Concluding remarks, 2nd and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. It says MDMA inactivates most liver CYP2D6 within about 2 hours and activity returns to its starting level only after at least 10 days (citing studies from 2008 and 2011), that phenocopying (the enzyme behaving as in a poor metabolizer whatever the genotype) was seen in 67% of male subjects in one study and 100% of females in another, and that the polymorphism and co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors may have less impact on the risk of acute toxicity than previously thought. The 67% is 10 of 15 men in the 2008 study read for this library, whose first probe dose was at 4 hours and whose ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days; the 100% for women (2011) was not read. The Concluding remarks also say carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects, which the review's body does not support with numbers.

risk_of_bias.note: The genotype comparison is observational and pooled across eight studies with unequal doses (ROBINS-E, some concerns; supplement not read); the probe-drug study is open, fixed-order and without a placebo MDMA session (RoB 2, high); the paroxetine trial is randomized (some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The studies point the same way; the review's 19% and 25% for a narrower genotype comparison differ from the paper's 15% headline.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy volunteers and for single doses; it says no second dose was given.

imprecision.note: Seven poor metabolizers, 15 men and 12 men; no confidence intervals for the main contrasts.

grade.reasoning: The central contrasts (genotype group, before and after one dose) are not randomized comparisons, so the claim starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status replicated: three independent lines (a pooled genotype analysis, a probe-drug study and CYP2D6-blocking medicines in a randomized trial and, as summarized, in others) agree that loss or blocking of CYP2D6 raises early MDMA levels by about 15 to 20 percent. The claim describes what was measured; it draws no conclusion about risk at any amount.

verification.flag_note: Carries the Mixing-page pair because it covers medicines that block CYP2D6; the editor may drop the pair if the claim should stay under pharmacology only. The narrative review (de la Torre et al., 2012) is a qualifying anchor only. Missing: Papaseit et al. (2012, ritonavir), Studerus et al. (2021) and the Yubero-Lahoz (2011) women's study have no reference records and were not read; the Schmid paper's supplement was not read. The reference record for O'Mathuna et al. (2008) gives pages 523-529 but the PDF prints 525-531; anchors here cite the PDF's printed pages.
